news.Title: Could Rivian's Model 3 Moment Be Coming? Tesla Stock Climbed 1,364% in 3 Years.
news.Content:
Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) investors have plenty riding on the recently launched and highly anticipated R2, and selling more vehicles would certainly be welcome. But the bigger prize is what could happen when the company gets more efficient at building them.

Fortunately, we have precedent from a fellow electric vehicle (EV) maker. Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) offers a compelling example. Its Model 3 production breakthrough helped set the stage for a much more profitable business -- and shareholders enjoyed a roller-coaster stock price ride along the way.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Could Rivian be approaching a similar turning point? There are encouraging signs, but the answer depends on more than customers wanting an R2. Let's dig in.

Rewind to Tesla's breakthrough

During the second quarter of 2018, Tesla's Model 3 gross margin turned slightly positive. Management credited lower labor hours, reduced ramp-up costs, better absorption of fixed costs, and lower material costs. Only one quarter later, Model 3 gross margin exceeded 20%, while labor hours per vehicle fell more than 30% sequentially. That happened even as Tesla shifted production toward more complex all-wheel-drive versions.

Tesla wasn't simply building more cars. It was using fewer labor hours to build each one . That doesn't necessarily mean its total labor hours declined, but it shows how a smoother production process can improve vehicle economics, requiring less labor time per vehicle.

Tesla's financial transformation quickly followed. Between the third quarter of 2018 and the third quarter of 2021, Tesla's company-wide operating margin increased from 6.1% to 14.6%. Between Sept. 28, 2018, and Sept. 30, 2021 -- the corresponding quarter-end trading dates -- its split-adjusted stock price climbed approximately 1,364%.

TSLA data by YCharts

Rivian shareholders would certainly take a helping of that, maybe even seconds. More importantly, Tesla's return reflected much more than one successful production ramp-up, and it certainly is not a forecast or prediction for Rivian. The useful lesson is how much the investment story can change when a promising vehicle becomes a profitable business.

Does Rivian have the demand?

Rivian will need ample demand to create its own Model 3 moment with its very own R2, and the early signals for R2 demand are encouraging. During its second-quarter earnings call, Rivian said reservation-to-order conversion for the roughly $58,000 R2 Launch Edition was meaningfully higher than management expected. It didn't disclose the conversion percentage, but that's a positive sign for the initial version before more affordable models of the R2 enter production.

Story Continues

Rivian subsequently delivered 19,248 vehicles across its lineup during the third quarter, increasing approximately 46% year over year and 58% sequentially. Production reached 19,751 vehicles, up approximately 57% from the second quarter. In other words, this R2 ramp-up is gathering momentum.

More importantly, management has identified the culprit behind less-than-perfect production. At September's Morgan Stanley conference, CEO RJ Scaringe said Rivian's factory was ahead of its supply base. Suppliers' ability to increase output was constraining the ramp-up, rather than the factory itself. He contrasted that with Tesla's initial Model 3 challenges inside its factory.

More than an R2 payoff

Investors might not have to wait for R3 or another future vehicle to benefit from Rivian's next manufacturing breakthrough. As R2 production accelerates, it could already improve the economics of the R1S, R1T, and commercial vans Rivian builds for Amazon .

How? Those vehicles share production shops with R2, and Rivian expects higher utilization to generate significant fixed-cost efficiencies. R2 wouldn't just bring another revenue stream -- it could help the factory earn its keep across multiple vehicles. That gives shareholders more riding on this ramp-up than R2 sales alone.

The good news for investors is that more benefits are on the way. Rivian started R2 production with one shift and planned to add a second by the end of the third quarter, with a third shift expected in 2027. That gives investors a timeline to watch.

What it all means

Investors should temper expectations of improvements during its upcoming third-quarter results , as launch costs and additional labor will still pressure automotive profitability. Rather, prepare to analyze fourth-quarter results for a clearer takeaway and track improvements throughout 2027. The next delivery record would be welcome, but improving automotive margins as production scales would be considerably more meaningful.

Tesla provides a powerful precedent. Rivian has to earn its own breakthrough -- and customers wanting R2 is only the beginning. Building it efficiently enough to improve the financial story is what could give shareholders something to truly celebrate over the next three years.

news.Title: Elon Musk Has Incredible News for Micron Stock Investors
news.Content:
Space Exploration Technologies and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk has given shares of Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) a terrific boost after his latest post on X, formerly Twitter.

While replying to a post by an analyst at Citrini Research, which provides thematic equity investing and macro trading insights, Musk pointed out that the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) needed in humanoid robots "will exceed everything else on Earth." Micron stock surged more than 5% following Musk's remark.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In this article, we will check if humanoids can indeed become the next major growth driver for the memory industry and Micron Technology.

Image source: Getty Images.

Robots can become the next big catalyst for the memory industry

According to Counterpoint Research, DRAM demand from humanoids could increase by almost 21x between 2026 and 2030. The research firm notes that the DRAM content in each humanoid could jump from the current 19GB to 39GB by the end of the decade.

However, Musk believes that humanoids will need much larger DRAM. Tesla , for instance, uses 72GB of memory on its AI5 chip that powers the Optimus robot, while the AI6 chip is equipped with 144GB of memory. It is worth noting that Musk had to slash the AI5's memory capacity in half, while the AI6 chip saw a one-third drop in memory capacity. Tesla had to make this move to procure enough memory volumes and reduce production costs amid the ongoing memory shortage.

What's worth noting is that Tesla has begun production of Optimus and intends to start shipping to customers next year. Musk predicts that Tesla can produce a million units of its humanoids every year at the Fremont factory. Moreover, demand for autonomous robots is increasing in factories.

Toyota , for instance, aims to automate its factories by deploying 400,000 robots. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs recently increased its humanoid sales forecast for 2035 by a whopping 5x. The investment bank estimates that shipments of humanoid robots could reach 6.5 million units in 2035, generating $138 billion in revenue.

As such, there is a strong likelihood that humanoids will sustain robust demand for memory chips over the long run, adding to existing catalysts such as data centers, smartphones, vehicles, and personal computers.

Story Continues

Investors may be making a mistake by not buying Micron stock

Micron stock has been in hot water lately. Concerns about the sustainability of heavy spending on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure have weighed on semiconductor stocks, but emerging niches such as humanoids and physical AI suggest that the memory market is poised to continue growing at a terrific pace over the long run.

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra noted on the recent earnings call that "physical AI can become a significant driver of memory and storage demand by the end of this decade," driven by increases in memory content and units. Importantly, Mehrotra notes that "several physical AI customers are sampling our next-generation products," and the size of the physical AI-focused memory market could increase substantially over the long run. According to Mehrotra:

Memory content in Level 4 and higher autonomous vehicles typically exceeds 200GB, while storage content reaches multiple terabytes, each more than an order of magnitude greater than in today's Level 2+ and Level 3 semi-autonomous vehicles. Humanoid robots are expected to have comparable memory and storage requirements to autonomous vehicles.

So, as AI moves beyond data centers into real-world applications, Micron's addressable market will grow substantially. This explains why buying this stock is a no-brainer right now. Micron trades at just 13 times earnings, while the forward earnings multiple of 5 is even more attractive. These multiples are extremely cheap for a company that's expected to clock a 133% increase in earnings per share in the current fiscal year.

Given that Micron already has solid catalysts driving phenomenal growth in revenue and earnings and is poised to win big from new opportunities such as physical AI, buying this AI stock at its current valuation will be a smart long-term move. And finally, Musk's latest statement on the state of the memory market could give Micron stock a much-needed boost after recent weakness.

news.Title: SpaceX Is Considering a Merger With Tesla. Here's Why That Would Be a Bad Move.
news.Content:
The final move may be about to unfold. Elon Musk has set plans in motion to potentially merge his two industrial giants: Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA). A merger has not been formally announced, but each company has formed an independent committee to explore the potential benefits of a merger. It is more likely than not to go through within the next year.

Two trillion-dollar market cap stocks merging would consummate the largest corporate marriage in history. I think it would be a terrible idea. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Minimal business overlap

Regardless of what the merger presentation says, there is little overlap between Tesla's and SpaceX's businesses today.

SpaceX has its launch business, connectivity (Starlink), and is investing in artificial intelligence ( AI ) data centers. It is investing in AI software services like Grok Bot in hopes of carving out a place in the AI race. Tesla sells electric vehicles and battery packs and is working on autonomous driving and humanoid robot technologies.

One might argue that the future Optimus humanoid robot could utilize Starlink to connect to the internet, or that Tesla battery packs could be used at SpaceX AI data centers. However, just because one business can sell a product to another does not mean the two should merge simply because they share the same chief executive officer.

Adding so many product lines under one corporate umbrella is not going to make the two businesses more valuable; it will muddy the waters and confuse any investor trying to decide whether to buy the stock.

Raiding Tesla's balance sheet for capital spending

SpaceX's revenue is soaring, posting 161% growth last quarter. Tesla, not so much. Its revenue was little changed year over year, with declining operating earnings, and its revenue has been stagnant for many years. Its earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) peaked in 2022 and have declined ever since.

So why does Musk want to merge it with SpaceX? It is likely due to the $45 billion in cash on Tesla's balance sheet. SpaceX is in the midst of a huge spending spree on data centers, which is a large cash drain for the business. This is why it did the biggest initial public offering (IPO) earlier this year, raised more debt in recent weeks, and might acquire Tesla.

Story Continues

Last quarter, SpaceX spent nearly $20 billion on capital expenditures, primarily for AI data centers. It plans to double this to $40 billion in Q4. Revenue was only $14.6 billion in Q3. If this level of capital spending continues, Tesla's balance sheet will likely be a good avenue to keep the party going.

The only question is at what price it is acquiring this cash.

SPCX Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts

The valuation math that should concern investors

Today, Tesla has a market cap of $1.6 trillion. For that, investors are buying a $100 billion revenue business with narrowing profit margins, now trading at a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 444. Maybe the electric vehicle business will revive, and maybe the promises made about autonomous driving and the Optimus humanoid robot will lead to explosive growth in the years ahead. Investors should have their doubts that this will occur anytime soon, as Musk has been making imminent promises in automation technology for more than a decade now, with few results.

It is not like SpaceX is a bargain stock, either, even though it is growing rapidly at the moment. With a market cap of about $2 trillion and $33 billion in trailing 12-month revenue, it has a price-to-sales ratio (P/S) of 59, which is one of the highest P/S ratios in the market today. Adding Tesla to the mix just to get its cash does not solve the issue.

Smart investors will avoid buying either stock. A merger will just make this situation messier.

news.Title: A SpaceX and Tesla Merger Will Only Be Successful If This One Thing Happens
news.Content:
Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) are both exploring a merger between the two companies. While both have been run separately by Elon Musk for years, the eccentric technology founder now believes it may be ideal to have the two businesses under one corporate umbrella. Each business has a separate committee exploring the prospects of a deal.

Increasingly, the companies are collaborating on projects, including the recently announced Terrafab semiconductor production venture. If a merger between the two companies is to be consummated, semiconductor manufacturing is key to lasting success. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Scaling chip production

Terrafab is just an idea today, a joint venture formed between SpaceX, Tesla, and Intel , with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing rumored to be in talks to join the project. Musk and the team have plans to build a massive manufacturing base in Texas for computer chips.

These chips will power the future of Tesla and SpaceX products and are a reason for the merger. These could include Tesla electric vehicles, the Optimus humanoid robot, Starlink satellites, and the data centers SpaceX is beginning to build for artificial intelligence ( AI ).

However, this is a long-term project, with production not planned until 2028 at the earliest. When this happens, SpaceX hopes to have engineered the ability to produce space-based data centers at a lower cost-to-serve than terrestrial competitors. If it can do so while powering these data centers with its own computer chips, this vertical integration could be a valuable competitive advantage for the combined SpaceX-Tesla business.

Tesla's financial state

The question remains: Why is Tesla needed for this space-based data center project, which is powered by internal computer chips? Sure, Tesla could use Terrafab's computer chips for its vehicles or to train its AI models for self-driving cars, but this isn't something it needs to do internally for the business to function, and it has nothing to do with SpaceX's ambitions.

What Musk and SpaceX likely want from Terrafab and the forthcoming Tesla and SpaceX merger is the cash on Tesla's balance sheet, which numbered $45 billion at the end of last quarter. However, the Tesla business itself is struggling, with operating income falling 56% last quarter. Revenue is not growing either, with promises of self-driving technology and the Optimus humanoid robot not appearing on today's financial statements.

Story Continues

It is not necessarily what SpaceX can do for Tesla, but what Tesla can provide to SpaceX in the form of capital, that is the reason for this merger exploration.

Should the two companies even merge?

If a Tesla-SpaceX merger occurs, much will rest on this Terrafab joint venture to ensure its success. It is part of a grand plan by Musk and SpaceX to build a massive orbital satellite and AI data center network. However, there are a ton of steps that need to occur before this happens, such as proving that Terrafab can actually manufacture working chips or getting orbital data centers functional.

Adding Tesla to the picture under one corporate umbrella might just make the story messier than it needs to be. There are many uncertainties in the story involving both companies. Sure, SpaceX could use Tesla's cash balance to fund its growth ambitions, but that should not be the only reason for a merger. Terrafab is an interesting idea, but all it is today -- along with many other business lines at Tesla and SpaceX -- is an idea, one that faces huge upfront capital commitments and technical challenges.

Plus, from an investor perspective, both stocks trade at premium valuations. Tesla's price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is in the hundreds, and SpaceX trades at a $2 trillion market cap compared to trailing revenue of $33 billion. A merger may make sense if you believe in the Terrafab project, but there are so many uncertainties across the board with these two businesses that I think both stocks are ones to avoid right now.

news.Title: SpaceX-Tesla Deal Faces Major China Problem
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

A potential SpaceX-Tesla merger may have a much bigger geopolitical problem than investors realize: China.

Bank of America said Beijing represents the main regulatory risk to any combination of Tesla ( NASDAQ:TSLA ) and SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ), even as the firm sees a deal as potentially positive for Tesla shareholders.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 8 Warning Signs with TSLA.

Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The core issue is Tesla's Shanghai plant.

According to BofA, the factory produces roughly half of Tesla's global vehicle output . If SpaceX acquired Tesla, that strategically important Chinese manufacturing base would suddenly sit inside a company controlled by one of the largest U.S. defense contractors.

That could draw intense scrutiny from Beijing.

BofA said press reports and public comments from Elon Musk indicate both Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to evaluate a transaction, although no terms have been agreed and a deal remains far from certain.

The bank believes one logical structure would be an all-stock acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX , with Tesla shareholders receiving newly issued SpaceX shares.

BofA also thinks Tesla shareholders could potentially negotiate a meaningful premium.

The firm said a 20% to 30% premium would still leave Musk with more than 50% of the combined company's voting power. Any transaction would need approval from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares, with abstentions and broker non-votes effectively counting against the proposal.

There is also a strategic case for combining the companies.

BofA highlighted Terafab , the companies' joint chip-manufacturing effort, as one of the clearest areas of overlap. Musk expects the project to cost more than $100 billion over time , and a merger could eliminate the need to negotiate how those costs are divided.

The companies already have commercial ties as well. SpaceX has purchased about $626 million of Tesla Megapacks so far this year.

Investor Takeaway

I think the most important part of BofA's note is that a SpaceX-Tesla merger would not be just a corporate-governance or valuation story.

It could become a U.S.-China regulatory story very quickly .

Tesla's Shanghai operation is too important to the company's global production footprint for Beijing to ignore a change in ownership that places it under a major U.S. defense contractor.

That does not mean China would block the transaction.

But it does introduce a geopolitical layer that could complicate approvals, deal structure and timing.

Story Continues

For investors, the key things to watch are whether formal merger terms emerge, how Tesla's Shanghai assets are treated, whether Chinese regulators signal concern, and what premium Tesla's special committee can negotiate .

BofA still rates Tesla Buy with a $460 price target .

The strategic case may be real.

The geopolitical hurdle could be just as real.

news.Title: Tesla Could Be About to Unlock a Brand-New Revenue Stream. Time to Buy the Stock?
news.Content: Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) has been a pioneer in the electric vehicle (EV) market, and the company still generates the lion's share of its revenue from this segment. However, the EV landscape has been somewhat uncertain in recent years, affecting Tesla's financial results. Thankfully, Tesla has several attractive potential growth opportunities, and the company could unlock a new revenue stream by the end of the year. Here's what investors need to know. Image source: The Motley Fool. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Could the Cybercab soon hit the proverbial shelves? In September, Tesla launched the Cybercab, an autonomous vehicle with two seats, no steering wheel, no pedals, and no mirrors. The Cybercab is an important piece in Tesla's robotaxi ambition. The vehicle is likely cheaper to manufacture than the Model Y and could generate sales over its entire useful life. The economics of Tesla's robotaxi business could be much more profitable than its consumer EV sales . Here is why. Tesla makes a significant amount of money every time it sells an EV, but annual sales after that are fairly modest -- they come from the $99 per month subscription to the company's Full Self-Driving (FSD) software. But Cybercabs, if used extensively, could generate thousands of dollars in revenue each year. Suppose each Cybercab accommodates 10 rides per day at an average price of $15 -- that's $150 every day, or $54,750 per year. And let's assume a 10-year useful life; that's $547,500 over the car's life. That's far more in sales than what Tesla can make from its most popular car, the Model Y, over its entire useful life. Our assumptions might turn out to be wrong, but the potential for Tesla's robotaxi fleet is there, and it helps explain why so many investors are excited about the company's future. However, Tesla has another plan in mind. In addition to running its own fleet of Cybercabs, the company wants to sell them to consumers and allow them to operate their own fleets. It intends to start selling the Cybercab by year-end. Tesla could then generate revenue from commissions on every ride booked through its network, or perhaps from FSD subscription fees, or maybe from repair and maintenance, although the company has not indicated that yet. Whatever the case may be, selling Cybercabs would allow the company to combine one benefit of its EV business -- upfront revenue from the sale of a car -- with the perks of its robotaxi fleet. There is also the possibility that Tesla will eventually sell its Cybercab to large corporations for a variety of purposes, such as delivering packages. Story Continues We are not there yet, of course, but the point is that Tesla's Cybercab could unlock highly lucrative monetization opportunities. Regulators might have a word to say Tesla's master plan might not go without a hitch. Shortly after the company launched the Cybercab, it became the subject of a safety probe by the U.S. Department of Transportation's National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Here is the short version. U.S. law allows automakers to self-certify compliance with federal vehicle safety standards. But those standards were designed for human-driven vehicles and generally require controls such as steering wheels and brake pedals. The NHTSA is investigating whether Tesla properly self-certified its Cybercab, which lacks these controls, potentially forcing the company to seek exemptions, modify the vehicle, or delay its commercial rollout. We aren't there yet, but it's a real risk worth monitoring for investors. My view is that, even with some setbacks, Tesla will likely be allowed to keep its Cybercabs on the road eventually, especially since the company is prioritizing safety. There has never been a fatal accident involving Tesla's robotaxi fleet. Meanwhile, the fleet is growing rapidly. As CEO Elon Musk pointed out, the Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown by a factor of 10 since its launch in September. Over the next few years, it could maintain a decent pace of growth, and provided utilization keeps up, revenue from this business could start meaningfully contributing to the company's top-line. But does that make the stock a buy? Not in my view, since the market has already factored the success of the Cybercab into the share price. Tesla is a great business, but at 159.8x forward earnings, and given the risks it faces from regulators and competitors, the stock looks a bit too risky. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook. Continue » Prosper Junior Bakiny has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. news.Title: Micron Became One of the 10 Biggest Holdings in S&P 500 Index Funds. What Does That Mean for the Stock?
news.Content:
Memory maker Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) now ranks among the biggest companies in the stock market. At the end of September, it was the ninth-largest holding in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT:VOO), making up 1.82% of the fund.

This put it above Tesla , at 1.52%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Funds made to track the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) hold the same stocks at around the same weights, so Micron's place shows up in all of them. The whole Vanguard fund, which has about $1.7 trillion in the ETF and its other share classes, owned about 29.7 million Micron shares on Sept. 30, or around 2.6% of the company.

The rise has been quick. Micron's market value passed $1 trillion for the first time on May 26, and the stock has more than quadrupled in the last year. But shares are also down about 8% since Sept. 30, to roughly $983 as I write. I think the weight itself matters less for the stock than it may seem.

Image source: Getty Images.

The weight follows the price

The S&P 500 is weighted by float-adjusted market value. That means S&P Dow Jones Indices counts the market value of each company's shares that are available to public investors, and a stock's weight is its share of that total.

Put another way, Micron's spot in the top 10 came from its stock price, which climbed much faster than the rest of the market.

That also explains how Micron passed Tesla . At the end of September, Tesla's shares were worth around $1.4 trillion all told, more than Micron's $1.2 trillion or so.

But Micron had the higher weight, because a far larger chunk of Tesla's stock falls outside what the index counts as available to the public.

The weight moves both ways, too. With Micron's shares down since Sept. 30, its weight in the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust was 1.54% on Oct. 26. That was below Tesla's 1.67%, and it put Micron just outside the top 10 that day.

Does the top 10 draw in more buyers?

Not on its own. After all, an index fund already holds every stock in proportion to its weight, so when Micron's price rises, the fund's stake gains value without the fund buying more shares.

Nothing new happens the day a stock moves from 11th place to ninth.

What does change is where new money goes. At a weight of around 1.6%, every $1,000 investors put into an S&P 500 fund now sends about $16 into Micron, much more than a year ago.

Story Continues

Of course, it works the other way, too. When money leaves these funds, their Micron holdings shrink in the same proportion. Index ownership hasn't kept the stock from sharp swings. Micron fell 6% on Oct. 22 alone, and it's about 19% under its record close, $1,213.56 on June 25.

Memory prices still matter most

Micron's stock, and its weight with it, climbed mostly because its earnings did, with demand from AI projects boosting its memory sales.

A year ago, the memory maker's quarterly revenue was $11.3 billion. Micron's fiscal 2026 ended on Sept. 3, and revenue in that year's last quarter reached $54.2 billion, up 379% year over year and 31% above the fiscal third quarter's $41.5 billion.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, management expects around $61.5 billion. Yes, that'd set another record. But it implies sequential growth of around 13%, a slowdown from the 31% rate of the last quarter.

Earnings per share for fiscal 2026 came to $74.33, up around 880% from $7.59 in fiscal 2025.

At around $983, the stock trades at about 13 times earnings, about half the 24.7 times earnings Vanguard listed for its S&P 500 fund at the end of September. Investors are paying much less for every dollar of Micron's profit than for the index overall, probably because memory prices have long moved in cycles.

For anyone who holds an S&P 500 fund, the top-10 spot mainly means Micron's swings show up more. A 10% fall in Micron would knock around 0.16% off the fund.

Does the top-10 spot change anything for the stock, then? Not much by itself. The index just gives Micron more weight when the stock beats the market and less when it trails. What moves the price is still memory demand.

And the company is still growing. At about 13 times earnings, I'd consider buying the shares. But anyone who holds an S&P 500 fund already has some Micron, and a fall in memory prices could hurt both.

news.Title: Tesla's Profits Took a Hit. Is It Building Something Worth the Cost?
news.Content:
Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) investors have plenty of reasons to look toward the future, and it could certainly be both wild and lucrative. Robotaxis, artificial intelligence (AI), and humanoid robots could open new revenue opportunities and an entirely different future -- the possibilities are exciting, no doubt about it.

But Tesla remains heavily dependent on selling electric vehicles (EVs) , and developing that future comes with a hefty bill. The EV maker's latest results show just how quickly that bill is growing. Third-quarter research and development (R&D) expenses jumped 69% year over year to $2.76 billion, while operating profit declined 56% to $718 million.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The question facing Tesla investors is a big one: Should they applaud the long-term investment or worry about the pressure on near-term earnings?

The bill is getting bigger

Tesla's third-quarter earnings pressure wasn't caused by a deteriorating automotive gross margin. Its automotive gross margin actually improved from 17% to 18.5% year over year, while companywide gross profit increased roughly 9%, from $5.05 billion to $5.49 billion. So what happened, you ask?

The trouble came further down the income statement. R&D expenses increased by $1.13 billion, more than twice the approximately $440 million increase in gross profit. Selling, general, and administrative expenses also rose. Together, those increases overwhelmed the improvement in gross profit and helped push operating profits lower.

Investors knew the bill for Tesla's sharp turn into more of a technology company, rather than a traditional EV maker, would come due over time. Tesla explained the R&D increase was largely due to costs associated with its AI development and other programs, including Optimus, silicon development, battery technologies, and new vehicles, as well as higher stock-based compensation, per Tesla's SEC filing.

There's an important mental note for investors to make here. This R&D spending is related to Tesla's broader investment push, but it isn't the same as capital expenditures. Tesla separately expects more than $20 billion in 2026 capex, including computing infrastructure, data centers, manufacturing facilities, and other long-lived assets.

The difference for investors is that R&D generally reduces earnings as incurred, while capital expenditures use cash up front and generally affect earnings over time through depreciation. Tesla faces both pressures as it builds toward its future, which could be wildly lucrative and also wildly expensive.

Story Continues

Spending isn't the same as succeeding

To be fair, cutting R&D spending just to make one quarter's earnings look better would likely be shortsighted -- which, unfortunately, Wall Street and big business can sometimes be. If Tesla's investments produce valuable technology and commercially successful products, accepting lower profits today could prove a great move for long-term investors.

That said, a larger research budget doesn't guarantee a successful product breakthrough, much-needed customer adoption, or improved profitability in the end.

Also, on the downside for investors, you might have considered operating profit improving from the second to the third quarter a silver lining, but that may not be the case. Operating profit improved from $398 million in the second quarter to $718 million in the third, but Tesla benefited from a one-time refund on tariffs during the third quarter. Even with that boost, operating profit was down significantly year over year.

What it all means

For long-term investors, the takeaway is pretty simple. Tesla's rising R&D expense helps explain today's operating profit pressure, even as automotive gross margin improved, but the spending itself doesn't validate tomorrow's growth story. Investors will want to watch for autonomous technology milestones , a growing number of paying customers for its future businesses, and evidence that new businesses can generate profits.

Tesla is spending heavily to build its future. Investors need that future to eventually start paying off, and that timeline is highly uncertain -- which is one word Wall Street, and most investors, don't like.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

news.Title: Rivian Post-Q3 Analysis: 3 Reasons Why the Stock is a Buy Now
news.Content:
For years, Rivian Automotive RIVN has been a story of promise more than execution. Big ambitions, heavy cash burn and persistent doubts about its ability to scale weighed on investor sentiment. But its third-quarter 2026 report suggests the narrative is starting to shift. Deliveries hit a record, losses were far narrower than expected, and the new R2 SUV is already the company's best seller. Here are the key highlights from the release, and why the stock deserves a place in your portfolio now.

RIVN's Q3 Earnings Snapshot

Rivian posted an adjusted loss of 48 cents per share, narrower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate and the year-ago loss of 65 cents per share. Revenues rose 38% year over year to $2.16 billion, beating estimates by 6.62%, driven by record vehicle deliveries, regulatory credits and software growth. Deliveries jumped 46% to 19,248 units.

Rivian Automotive, Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Rivian Automotive, Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Rivian Automotive, Inc. Quote

Rivian's closest peer, Lucid Group LCID, delivered 3,806 vehicles, which fell short of analyst estimates and were down 6.6% on a yearly basis and 3.7% sequentially. Meanwhile, EV giant Tesla TSLA delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, up 1.3% sequentially but down 2.1% on a year-over-year basis. While Tesla delivered third-quarter earnings beat, Lucid is set to report results on Nov. 9.

Rivian's automotive revenues grew 36%, while software and services revenues climbed 45%. Consolidated gross profit improved to $176 million but free cash outflow widened to $1.12 billion, underscoring that Rivian is still investing heavily to scale.

Why Rivian's Story Is Getting Interesting

R2 Is Fueling a Demand-Led Growth Story :The R2 SUV overtook the R1 and the electric delivery vans to become Rivian's best-selling vehicle in just its first quarter of meaningful volume. The early signals are encouraging—strong reservation conversion and more than 103,000 demo drives show real consumer curiosity.

Rivian is also adding capacity. A second production shift at its Normal facility should lift output and manufacturing efficiency. Management raised full-year 2026 delivery guidance to 67,000-70,000 units from 65,000-70,000, and expects R2 to make up the majority of fourth-quarter deliveries.

Software and services add a second engine. Revenues are growing through development work under the Volkswagen joint venture, vehicle maintenance and the Autonomy+ subscription. Paid software features create recurring revenues that do not depend on selling a new car each time.

Story Continues

These factors are expected to drive Rivian's revenue trajectory, with the Zacks Consensus Estimate implying year-over-year growth of 37% in 2026 and 56% in 2027.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Cost Discipline Is Showing Up in the Numbers : Sales growth matters if losses shrink alongside it, and this is where Rivian impressed most. Automotive cost of goods sold per vehicle improved by more than $12,000 sequentially, helped by a richer R2 mix and better factory utilization. Simpler vehicle components, better logistics and tougher supplier negotiations are all feeding in.

As volumes rise, fixed manufacturing costs get spread across more vehicles, which should strengthen unit economics. Management expects R2 to reach positive gross margin by the end of 2026. Rivian also tightened its adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $1.75-$1.85 billion, a $100 million improvement at the midpoint.

The consensus mark expects the loss per share to narrow 8% in 2026 and 20% in 2027 on a year-over-year basis. Scale is the key. Rivian has to scale beyond its current R2 production plan of 160,000 units to reach overall profitability, a ramp management calls critical to positive gross margin across the business.

Autonomy Offers Long-Term Upside : This could change how investors value the company. Rivian's Autonomy+ adoption is running ahead of management's expectations. A limited rollout of Point to Point driving is planned for late 2026, with wider availability in 2027.

Rivian's acquisition of Third Dimension AI should speed up autonomous development through better simulation and model validation. Its Uber partnership provides another growth avenue, with Level 4 autonomous R2 robotaxis planned from 2028. Uber is expected to invest another $250 million upon hitting milestones by the end of 2026, with up to $700 million more tied to milestones through 2031.

Rivian's vertically integrated hardware and software stack should let it develop this technology across both consumer and commercial vehicles. That could diversify revenues well beyond vehicle sales, though execution remains critical.

Bottom Line

Rivian's third quarter shows a business gaining real operating traction, with growth and cost control finally moving in the same direction.Revenues are accelerating, losses are narrowing faster than analysts expected, unit costs are falling, and a hit product is gaining traction. Autonomy adds a long-term growth option.

That said, risks are real. Cash burn is still heavy, profitability depends on a successful R2 ramp, and the autonomy payoff is years away.

But with raised guidance and narrowing losses, the risk-reward looks increasingly favorable for investors with a long-term view. If you are ready for some volatility, Rivian looks like a stock worth buying now.

RIVN currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here .

news.Title: Why Beijing could block the SpaceX-Tesla merger
news.Content:
Investing.com -- Bank of America says China is the main regulatory risk to a potential combination of Tesla and SpaceX, though it sees a deal as incremental upside for Tesla shareholders.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

"According to press reports and public comments by Musk, Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to evaluate a transaction, although terms have not been agreed and a transaction is far from certain," wrote BofA.

"We view China as the main regulatory risk as a potential deal would place Tesla's Shanghai plant, which builds roughly half of its global vehicle output, under a major U.S. defense contractor."

BofA said a logical structure would be an all-stock acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX, with Tesla shareholders receiving newly issued SpaceX shares.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

"The key question, in our view, is whether TSLA's special committee can negotiate a premium, which we think is likely given Tesla's core auto momentum and robotaxi inflection," BofA said.

A 20% to 30% premium would still leave Musk with more than 50% of the combined entity's voting power. Any deal would need approval from a majority of all outstanding Tesla shares, with abstentions and broker non-votes counting against it.

The bank said the strategic case centers on AI, particularly Terafab, the companies' joint chip-manufacturing effort.

Musk expects Terafab's costs to exceed $100 billion over the long term, and a merger would remove the need to negotiate a cost split. The companies also have existing product ties, and SpaceX has bought $626 million of Tesla Megapacks so far this year.

BofA maintained its Buy rating and $460 price target on Tesla, expecting robotaxis to become a meaningful earnings driver by the end of 2027.

news.Title: ORLY Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on Strong Sales & Tariff Refunds
news.Content:
O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. ORLY reported third-quarter 2026 earnings of 97 cents per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 92 cents by 5.44%. Earnings increased 14% from 85 cents in the year-ago quarter, supported by robust sales growth and tariff refunds.

Revenues rose 9% year over year to $5.12 billion, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $5 billion by 2.49%. Comparable store sales increased 7.2%, reflecting double-digit growth in the professional business and mid-single-digit growth in the do-it-yourself (DIY) business.

O'Reilly currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. Quote

ORLY's Professional Business Drives Sales Growth

Sales to professional service provider customers increased 12.7% year over year to $2.60 billion from $2.31 billion. Professional comparable store sales grew slightly more than 10%, making the business the largest contributor to overall comparable sales growth.

Growth in professional comparable sales was evenly split between higher average ticket values and increased transaction counts. Professional customer transactions rose at a mid-single-digit rate, reflecting market share gains. New stores opened in 2025 and 2026 contributed $94 million in incremental sales during the quarter.

O'Reilly's DIY Sales Gain Despite Consumer Pressure

Sales to DIY customers increased 6.2% year over year to $2.45 billion from $2.30 billion. Comparable sales in the retail business grew at a mid-single-digit rate, benefiting from stronger demand for hot weather-related products and higher average ticket values.

DIY transaction counts faced a low-single-digit headwind, indicating pressure on consumers. However, higher ticket values more than offset the decline. Same-SKU inflation exceeded 4% across the combined businesses, primarily driven by petroleum-based products such as motor oil and lubricants.

Management noted that consumers continued prioritizing vehicle maintenance and repair, although lower-income DIY customers remained under greater pressure than higher-income and professional service customers.

ORLY's Margins Expand on Tariff Refund Benefits

Gross profit increased 10% year over year to $2.68 billion from $2.44 billion. Gross margin expanded 50 basis points to 52.4%, primarily benefiting from $39 million in tariff refunds received through supplier partners. These refunds contributed 76 basis points to the gross margin rate.

Story Continues

However, petroleum-based categories created approximately 40 basis points of gross margin pressure due to unfavorable product mix and pricing dynamics. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased 8% to $1.58 billion but declined to 30.9% of sales from 31.1%.

Operating income climbed 13% to $1.10 billion, with operating margin improving to 21.4% from 20.7%. Net income increased 8% to $786 million from $726 million.

O'Reilly Expands Its Store Network

The company opened 63 new stores across North America during the third quarter, including 54 domestic locations, eight in Mexico and one in Canada. Its total store count reached 6,758 as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Year-to-date net new store openings totaled 173. Management remains confident of achieving its 2026 target of 225-235 openings and announced plans to accelerate expansion to 265-275 net new stores in 2027.

The company continues investing in distribution capacity and automation to support expansion, improve product availability and enhance service efficiency.

ORLY's Cash Flow Strengthens, Buybacks Continue

O'Reilly generated $2.60 billion in operating cash flow during the first nine months of 2026, up from $2.13 billion a year earlier. Capital expenditures totaled $860 million, while free cash flow increased to $1.73 billion from $1.20 billion.

Cash and cash equivalents totaled $194.4 million as of Sept. 30, 2026. Long-term debt was $7.71 billion, compared with $6.02 billion at 2025-end.

During the quarter, the company repurchased 11.8 million shares for $1.03 billion. Approximately $727 million remained available under its repurchase authorization as of Oct. 28, 2026.

O'Reilly Raises 2026 Earnings and Margin Outlook

For 2026, management raised its comparable store sales growth guidance to 5.5-6.5% from 4-6%. Total revenues are projected between $19 billion and $19.3 billion.

Gross margin guidance increased to 51.6-52.1%, while operating margin expectations rose to 19.5-20%. The company now anticipates earnings of $3.25-$3.35 per share.

Operating cash flow is projected at $3.2-$3.6 billion, with capital expenditures of $1.3-$1.4 billion. Free cash flow guidance increased to $1.9-$2.2 billion.

Management expects fourth-quarter gross margin to moderate from the third quarter's tariff-refund-supported level. Same-SKU inflation is also expected to ease, while higher fuel costs and operating expenses could remain near-term pressures.

Other Key Releases From the Auto Space

Genuine Parts Company GPC reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of $2.07 per share, which missed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $2.09. The bottom line increased 4.5% from $1.98 in the year-ago quarter. Revenues rose 4.2% year over year to $6.52 billion and surpassed the consensus estimate of $6.5 billion. Comparable sales increased 2.9%, led by strong Industrial demand. Genuine Parts ended September with $2.4 billion of liquidity, including $763 million in cash.

General Motors GM delivered strong third-quarter 2026 results yesterday. Its earnings per share grew 32.2% year over year to $3.70 and topped the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.55. Revenues of $50.02 billion increased 3% year over year and outpaced the consensus mark of $48.21 billion. On a further encouraging note, General Motors raised its adjusted automotive free cash flow forecast to $11.5-$12.5 billion from $9.5-$11.5 billion and authorized a $20-billion multi-year share repurchase program.

Tesla TSLA reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of 48 cents per share, which beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 45 cents by 6.67%. However, earnings declined 4% from 50 cents in the year-ago quarter, reflecting higher operating expenses. Tesla's revenues totaled $28.05 billion, down marginally from $28.1 billion a year ago. The metric surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $27.78 billion by 0.96%. Tesla has trimmed its 2026 capital expenditure outlook to approximately $20 billion from $25 billion guided earlier.

news.Title: Are Wall Street Analysts Bullish on Tesla Stock?
news.Content:
Valued at a market capitalization of $1.6 trillion, Tesla, Inc. (TSLA) is an electric vehicle and clean energy company that designs and manufactures electric cars, battery energy storage systems, and solar energy products. The Texas-based company is also expanding into autonomous driving, robotaxis, and artificial intelligence.

Tesla has struggled to win over investors amid intensifying competition in the EV market, with shares tumbling 12.6% over the past 52 weeks, sharply underperforming the S&P 500 Index ($SPX), which has gained 12% over the same time frame. Over the past six months, however, both the stock and the index have rallied 8.2%.

More News from Barchart

Elon Musk Invests $1 Billion in Skydance Stock. He Could Be Setting the Stage for a Major Starlink Deal.

'I Still Live A Great Life': Floyd Mayweather Says a Man 'Acting Like He Was A Friend' Stole $200 Million From Him

The sector-specific State Street Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLY) is down 2.8% over the past 52 weeks, outperforming Tesla, but has dipped marginally over the past six months, trailing the stock.

Tesla shares popped 3.4% on Oct. 21, after the company delivered a mixed third-quarter 2026 performance, beating analysts' earnings expectations and improving automotive margins, but continued to face pressure from rising operating expenses, declining energy revenue, and substantial investments in autonomous driving and AI.

It reported adjusted earnings of $0.48 per share, exceeding analysts' consensus estimate of $0.45. Revenue, however, remained essentially unchanged at $28.05 billion. Gross profit increased 8.7% to $5.49 billion, lifting the gross margin to 19.6% from 18% a year earlier. Yet operating expenses surged 39.2% to $4.78 billion, dragging operating income down 55.8% to $718 million.

On the vehicle front, Tesla produced 464,391 vehicles and delivered 486,532 during the quarter, but automotive revenue slipped 3% to $20.56 billion. Services and other revenue provided a bright spot, climbing 32.5% to $4.61 billion. Tesla's autonomous-driving ambitions remained firmly in focus, as investors assessed whether growing demand for Full Self-Driving software and progress in robotaxis could unlock new revenue streams and offset rising investment costs.

For FY2026 ending in December, Wall Street analysts expect Tesla's EPS to decrease by 38.5 YOY to $0.67 on a diluted basis. However, EPS is expected to rebound and improve 61.2% year over year to $1.68 in fiscal 2027.

Story Continues

Among the 41 Wall Street analysts covering TSLA's stock, the consensus is a "Moderate Buy." That's based on 16 "Strong Buy" ratings, two "Moderate Buys," 20 "Holds," and three "Strong Sells."

The ratings configuration is more bullish than it was a month ago, with 15 "Strong Buy" suggestions.

On Oct. 24, Bank of America maintained its "Buy" rating on Tesla and reaffirmed its $460 price target, signaling confidence in the EV maker's long-term growth prospects. However, the bank lowered its 2027 earnings estimate by 8.4%, citing elevated research and development spending ahead of upcoming product launches.

Tesla's mean price target of $413.91 indicates a 2.6% downside from current market prices. However, the Street-high price target of $600 implies a potential upside of 48.8%.

news.Title: CVNA Q3 Earnings Miss on Higher Costs Despite Record Sales
news.Content:
Carvana Co. CVNA reported earnings of 39 cents per share for the third quarter of 2026, missing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 47 cents. Earnings rose 85.7% year over year. Revenues of $8.04 billion increased 42.4% year over year and surpassed the consensus mark of $7.67 billion. The top-line beat reflected record retail volumes and higher vehicle sales revenues.

Retail units sold advanced 38.9% to a record 217,385, marking the company's first quarter above 200,000 units. Strong volume growth supported record profitability, although higher logistics costs and rising benchmark interest rates pressured unit economics.

Carvana Co. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Carvana Co. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Carvana Co. Quote

CVNA's Retail Volume and Sales Revenues Surge

Retail vehicle sales increased 53.8% to $6.14 billion, supported by higher transaction volumes and vehicle pricing. Retail revenue per unit rose to $28,263 from $25,625 a year ago. The company continued gaining market share as the broader automotive retail industry remained approximately flat.

Wholesale sales and revenues increased 10.6% to $1.30 billion. Wholesale vehicle unit sales climbed to 111,119 from 80,369. Other sales and revenues grew 25.3% to $594 million, reflecting continued growth in the company's complementary revenue streams.

Carvana's Gross Profit Rises, Unit Economics Soften

Total gross profit increased 32.5% to $1.52 billion. Retail vehicle gross profit advanced to $773 million from $540 million, while wholesale gross profit declined to $154 million from $135 million.

Wholesale gross profit rose 14.1% to $154 million from $135 million, while other gross profit increased 25.3% to $594 million.

However, total gross profit per unit (GPU) declined $365 to $6,997, while non-GAAP GPU fell $410 to $7,093. Non-GAAP retail GPU increased $85 to $3,625, supported by wider spreads between retail and wholesale prices. Non-GAAP wholesale GPU declined $196 to $759, while non-GAAP other GPU decreased $299 to $2,709, reflecting lower customer financing rates relative to benchmarks and rising market interest rates.

CVNA's Expenses Rise, EBITDA Margin Contracts

Selling, general and administrative expenses increased 35.3% to $805 million from $595 million. Higher advertising, fuel and logistics costs drove the increase. However, SG&A expenses per retail unit declined to $3,703 from $3,816, reflecting improved overhead leverage as volumes expanded.

Operating income increased 29.3% to $714 million, although the operating margin contracted to 8.9% from 9.8%. Adjusted EBITDA rose 25.6% to a record $800 million, while the adjusted EBITDA margin narrowed to 10% from 11.3%. Net income increased 83.7% to $483 million, despite a $53 million loss associated with debt extinguishment. Net income margin expanded to 6% from 4.7%.

Story Continues

Carvana Expands Production Capacity

Carvana continued expanding its vehicle reconditioning infrastructure to support future growth. During the quarter, the company integrated retail production capabilities at two additional ADESA locations, bringing the total number of integrated sites to 21. It also began construction on two additional full buildouts.

The company currently has three full buildout sites under construction, all expected to begin production in 2027. Its existing footprint provides fully built-out annual production capacity of approximately 1.5 million retail units, with sufficient real estate to eventually support 3 million units annually.

Management highlighted improvements in production efficiency, with quarterly vehicle production exceeding 200,000 units for the first time.

CVNA's Cash Position and Liquidity Strengthen

Cash and cash equivalents totaled $3.05 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026, compared with $2.33 billion at year-end 2025. Total assets increased to $15.20 billion from $13.20 billion, while vehicle inventory rose to $3.46 billion from $2.41 billion.

For the first nine months of 2026, net cash provided by operating activities increased to $900 million from $606 million a year earlier. Capital expenditures totaled $166 million compared with $96 million in the year-ago period.

During the third quarter, Carvana refinanced $1.7 billion of senior secured notes due 2030 through a senior secured term loan, generating approximately $45 million in annual interest expense savings. Its net debt-to-trailing-12-month adjusted EBITDA ratio improved to 0.8 times, while adjusted EBITDA-to-interest expense coverage reached 6.9 times.

Carvana Raises 2026 EBITDA Expectations

For the fourth quarter, management expects retail units sold to increase sequentially, assuming stable market conditions. The company now anticipates adjusted EBITDA at the higher end of its previously communicated full-year 2026 guidance of $2.7-$3 billion.

Carvana also reiterated its goal of selling 3 million retail vehicles annually between 2030 and 2035. Beginning in 2027, management plans to shift its primary reporting focus toward GAAP profitability metrics, replacing its 13.5% adjusted EBITDA margin target with an equivalent 12.5% operating margin objective.

Starting with its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, Carvana plans to discontinue quarterly and annual financial outlooks, focusing instead on progress toward its longer-term operational and profitability targets.

news.Title: The 'Magnificent 7' stocks are seeing stunning declines
news.Content:
Call it the Unflattering Seven.

Long known as the "Magnificent Seven" stocks, Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Nvidia ( NVDA ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Tesla ( TSLA ), Meta ( META ), and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) shares are acting anything but, especially compared to their 52-week highs.

Meta and Alphabet are effectively in bear markets, down more than 20% from their 52-week highs, as the Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace graphic below shows. Tesla is off by 19.2%, Amazon by 15.1%, and AI chip darling Nvidia by 12.2%.

Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, and Tesla have been crushed following earnings reports that showed pressured free cash flow amid aggressive AI spending. Nvidia is down due to fears that all these hyperscalers are overspending and will be forced to pull back in 2027.

Apple and Microsoft are the only Magnificent Seven names hanging tough, for company-specific reasons.

Microsoft managed to show positive free cash flow this week alongside strong Azure sales growth. Apple isn't being viewed as an AI play, but more as a cash-rich play rolling out new hardware in the iPhone and Mac realms.

"There is too much weakness in tech for the market to ignore," BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky said.

Too much weakness in seven of the world's most important stocks for the market to ignore is more like it.

news.Title: The Case Against a SpaceX and Tesla Merger
news.Content:
While we don't know what terms, if any, are on the table for a potential merger, there's a strong case that now isn't the best time for Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) to pursue a merger with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX). The argument rests on two main ideas. First, it runs contrary to market trends; second, Tesla is on the cusp of delivering significant shareholder value after years of disappointment.

Different risk and capital profiles

Over the last decade, the major trend with industrial conglomerates such as General Electric, United Technologies Corporation, Honeywell , 3M , Danaher , Johnson Controls , and Emerson Electric has been to break them up. While each company had its own circumstances, three themes apply to all:

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Separating companies allows for greater management and operational focus.

The market has tended to apply a so-called conglomerate discount, and investors increasingly value the ability to make targeted investments.

Each company has its own specific risk and its own capital allocation priorities, and they are better served as stand-alone companies.

Given the incredible complexity inherent in managing Tesla (EVs, robotaxi/Cybercab, Optimus, energy generation/storage, charging infrastructure, and a host of investments in building its own supply chain) and SpaceX (launch services, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, Starlink, defense networks), it's not hard to see how complex a merged entity would become.

The argument over the conglomerate discount is admittedly subject to change, as conglomerates once commanded a premium. However, that's not the case now, and until it changes, there's no strong reason to believe a merger will lead to an immediate market-valuation rerating of the merged entity. On the contrary, the opposite could occur.

Different risk profiles and capital profiles

The argument from specific risk and capital profiles is the strongest. Tesla is on the cusp of beginning a multiyear journey to scale its robotaxi service and generate a long stream of recurring revenue from robotaxi/Cybercab. Investors can disagree on its profit potential amid competition, but robotaxi/Cybercab is baked into the valuation, and if you are holding the stock, you presumably believe in the potential of autonomous driving.

Story Continues

While it will obviously require significant upfront capital investment to build out the network, Tesla has the resources to do so and create a company with significant long-term cash flows. The same argument, albeit a few more years out, applies to Optimus. Tesla does not need SpaceX to achieve its own goals.

In contrast, SpaceX operates in a high-risk sector that requires even more massive capital investment. Moreover, while Starlink is currently SpaceX's profit generator, its revenue driver is the Super Intelligence business. The former is effectively funding growth in the latter.

Tesla is moving toward becoming a company with a long-term stream of recurring revenue, scaling robotaxi/Cybercab and, in time, Optimus, and a play on physical AI. In contrast, SpaceX is a business that requires massive, ongoing, and uncertain capital expenditures and is a play on AI infrastructure.

Regarding the uncertainty of capital expenditures, consider orbital data centers and SpaceX. Their depreciation rate is likely to be high because they realistically can't be serviced in space and, unlike terrestrial data centers, which can replace servers and chips, will likely last only as long as their graphics processing units (GPUs) remain useful. A high depreciation rate implies higher maintenance capital spending.

Tesla hasn't released value from robotaxi/Cybercab yet

To understand this argument, consider how private equity might run Tesla. Their typical model is to generate value from the investment and sell the asset only once the business is firing on all cylinders, and it can optimize the price.

If you believe Tesla will evolve into a company generating billions of recurring revenue from its Cybercab fleet and then from Optimus, it makes sense to hold the asset, at least until the company proves the doubters wrong and releases value from the robotaxi rollout. At which point, Tesla shareholders will be in a stronger position to demand a healthier premium for the business.

What it means to investors

Again, while it's true that we don't know what kind of offer or what deal it will be, or even if there will be a proposal at all, the reality is the value of Tesla will key off of its current market price, and if you think it's undervalued and/or want to wait until the company releases value from robotaxi, then an offer now is unlikely to lead to a favorable outcome for you.

All told, in a merger, Tesla investors would dilute their claim on cash flows from robotaxi, EVs, and robotics (physical AI) in favor of using that cash to support space exploration and cloud computing (AI infrastructure). This creates a merged company with a significantly different risk and capital-allocation profile from Tesla, and they might not get full value for their Tesla shares until robotaxi scales.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »
